Stage 3 · Reading

The house with no spare bedroom

An article on shared living, and on what a community does with the rooms nobody uses.

🛌🌱
1 · Before you read. Which of these would you find hardest to share with your neighbours?

Choose one and say why. Compare with a partner before you read.Choose one and say why before you read.Choose one and note your reason. You will check it against the text.

The house with no spare bedroom

Written for this course, from published research on Danish and Dutch cohousing (Choi, European Planning Studies, 2004; Brenton, on schemes in Denmark and the Netherlands) and from the UK Cohousing Network.

1Most of the houses built in Europe over the last century contain a room that is used for about nine nights a year. A few families use the spare bedroom more than that; hardly any use it enough to justify heating it, cleaning it and paying a mortgage on it. Multiply that by every household in a neighbourhood and the waste stops looking like a private eccentricity and starts looking like a planning problem.

2Co-housing starts from exactly this observation. Each family owns or rents a private property, with its own kitchen and its own front door, and every resident can shut that door on the rest of the world. What the households do not each own is a guest room, a laundry, a workshop or an entertainment space. There is one of each, shared, and both the cost and the cleaning are divided among all of them. The private dwellings are usually smaller than average on purpose, because the money saved goes into the common house instead. Almost every scheme has one, and almost every common house has a kitchen, a dining room and a laundry in it.

3Neither the idea nor the arithmetic is new. The first modern scheme opened north of Copenhagen in 1972, after its architect’s earlier attempt had collapsed in the face of neighbours’ objections; twenty-seven households moved in, and a second Danish project followed a year later. Several hundred communities now exist across northern Europe, and the Netherlands alone has more than three hundred. Most of them were designed by the people who were going to live in them, which is slow, and which is also the point: residents who have argued for two years about where to put the bins tend to know their neighbours.

4What has changed is who applies. Most of the early residents were young families looking for somewhere the children could be watched by more than two adults. A large number of applicants now are people over seventy who want to go on living independently, in a property they control, and who know perfectly well what the alternative looks like. Studies of senior schemes in Denmark, Sweden and the Netherlands report the same finding: the dominant motive is not practical help but the avoidance of isolation. Several of them also record higher levels of social and physical activity among residents than among comparable people living alone.

5None of this suits everybody, and the literature is honest about that. Some of the meetings are long, and a few of them are about washing machines. Decisions taken by consensus can take months. Residents eat separately most nights, and plenty of them say the shared meals are the part they would give up first. Cohousing also tends to attract people with time, confidence and a university education, which limits how far it can be offered as a general answer to anything.

6But almost all of them mention the same thing, and it is not the guest room. Somebody notices when your curtains stay shut. In a period that has seen a steady rise in one-person households across Europe, and growth in the number of people studying and working at home through distance learning, that is not a small claim. The spare bedroom was never really the problem. It was the clearest sign of a way of building that assumed everyone would rather be left alone.

1 · Read the explanation.
Two decisions in one word

A quantifier answers two questions at once. First, how many or how much — and here English cares whether the noun is countable (many houses) or uncountable (much space). Second, which ones — are you talking about a class of things in general, or about a particular group?

That second question is what the little word of is for. Most residents like it is a claim about residents everywhere. Most of the residents like it is a claim about the people in this scheme. Use of whenever the next word is the, my, these, those, or a pronoun: most of them, never most them.

The distinctions that carry meaning
  • a few / few. A few is positive: there are some. Few is negative: there are not enough. The same applies to a little and little with uncountable nouns.
  • every / each. Both take a singular noun and a singular verb. Every looks at the whole group; each looks at the members one by one.
  • both / either / neither. These are only for two. Neither is already negative, so do not add another negative to the verb.
  • none of. Formal writing takes a singular verb after it, although a plural is common in speech.
  • much is rare in positive statements. We have much space sounds odd; say plenty of space or a great deal of space.

Two things to watch

1 — Of is not optional in front of the. Most of the residents, none of this, all of them. But no of when the noun stands alone: most residents, all houses.

2 — One negative is enough. Neither of them was interested, not neither of them wasn’t interested. The same applies after none and hardly any.

11 · Read this before the extra practice.
The article the quantifier hides

Quantifiers do two jobs at once. They say how many or how much, and they say whether you mean a particular group or not. Most housing is built for families is a claim about housing in general; Most of the houses here have a spare room is about a particular set. The rule is mechanical: add of the (or of my, of these) as soon as you narrow the group, and drop it when you do not. The same applies to all, some, many, few, several, none.

The difference between a few and few is not quantity but attitude. A few families use the spare room says there are some, and that is worth noting. Few families use it says there are hardly any, and that is a problem. The uncountable pair works the same way: a little space against little space. In speech, few and little alone sound formal; hardly any is the everyday version.

Countable, uncountable, and the ones that trip people

Countable only: many, a few, few, several, both, either, neither, every, each, a large number of. Uncountable only: much, a little, little, a great deal of, a large amount of. Either: some, any, plenty of, most, all, a lot of, hardly any, none. Note that much in a positive statement sounds odd in speech — We have a lot of time, not much time, though much is fine in questions and negatives.

Every and each both take a singular verb: Every household has its own front door. Every looks at the group as a whole; each looks at the members one at a time, and only each can stand alone (Each of them owns the property). Both, either and neither are for exactly two: Both the cost and the cleaning are shared · Neither scheme works without a caretaker.

Errors to watch: Most of people → Most people or most of the people · Every households have → Every household has · a few money → a little money · He has many informations — information is uncountable: a great deal of information.

1 · Read the model.
Model · a note to all fourteen households

At Tuesday’s meeting the group agreed to build the guest wing and the laundry, and to leave the rest of the land as garden. Neither the entertainment space nor the workshop will go ahead this year.

The reasoning was straightforward. Most of the households said they would use a guest room several times a year, and hardly any of us has space for visitors indoors. Every property loses about four square metres to a washing machine, so a shared laundry gives fourteen families a room back. Few of the households, by contrast, expected to use an entertainment space more than once a month, and a large number of us pointed out that the common hall already does that job on Sundays.

None of this is fixed for ever. Both decisions will be reviewed after two years, and there is still plenty of room at the north end if the balance turns out to be wrong. A few of you asked about noise: that is on the agenda for the next meeting rather than this one.
